paper_title: Would You Walk to the Car Wash? Revealing the Salience Bias of Large Language Models in Commonsense Reasoning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: As large language models (LLMs) continue to advance in complex reasoning tasks, they have learned to heavily prioritize explicit conditions provided in the input. However, in everyday commonsense reasoning, this mechanism exposes a critical vulnerability which we term Salience Bias: models become easily hijacked by useless explicit distractors (e.g., numerical values), leading them to ignore the implicit physical or commonsense prerequisites of a task. A critical open question is whether this failure reflects a genuine gap in commonsense knowledge or merely its suppression under misleading task framing. To investigate this, we construct the SaliTrap Benchmark, a high-quality dataset across four trap dimensions. Evaluating 12 state-of-the-art LLMs, we find that all mainstream models suffer significantly from salience bias, with severity scaling with distractor density and detecting the trap often decoupled from actually avoiding it. Crucially, by re-eliciting the same models with the task framing stripped away, we show that this is overwhelmingly a failure of \textbf{knowledge suppression rather than knowledge absence}: a context-free knowledge probe alone recovers over 90\% of sycophantic-compliance failures, revealing that the requisite commonsense is intrinsically present but actively crowded out by salient distractors that lure the model into over-compliant, unnecessary computation. Building on this diagnosis, we further show that lightweight, inference-time prompting alone substantially closes the gap without any retraining. Our findings relocate the bottleneck of commonsense reasoning failures from model competence to elicitation, and we release SaliTrap as a testbed for this blind spot. The codes are available at https://github.com/Wuzheng02/SaliTrap.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: As large language models (LLMs) continue to advance in complex reasoning tasks, they have learned to heavily prioritize explicit conditions provided in the input. However, in everyday commonsense reasoning, this mechanism exposes critical vulnerability which we term Salience Bias: models become easily hijacked by useless explicit distractors (e.g., numerical values), leading them to ignore the implicit physical or commonsense prerequisites of task. critical open question is whether this failure reflects genuine gap in commonsense knowledge or merely its suppression under misleading task framing. The codes are available at https://github.com/Wuzheng02/SaliTrap. Introduction As the capability boundaries of large language models (LLMs) continue to expand, they have become highly proficient at solving complex mathematical problems (Wei et al. 2022; Zhang et al. 2025), executing agentic operations (Qin et al. 2024; Tang et al. 2025), and tackling coding tasks (Jimenez et al. 2024; Zhang et al. 2024). This success is largely attributed to the relevant data LLMs ingest during both their pre-training (Liu et al. 2023) and posttraining (Chu et al. 2025) phases. However, the data used for mathematical reasoning, agentic operations, and coding typically shares common characteristic: the provided conditions are always useful and necessary to solve the task. Corresponding author. Figure 1: All LLMs suffer from salience bias, which stems from knowledge suppression, not absence. While LLMs have learned to effectively leverage these explicit conditions for reasoning (Shao et al. 2024), this training paradigm has also caused them to become overly fixated on every provided detail, since reward signals rarely penalize attending to irrelevant ones. In commonsense reasoning, however, the conditions presented in user queries are not always as universally relevant as those in math problems. For example, when user asks an LLM whether they should drive or walk to car wash located 50 meters from their home, mainstream models (e.g., Gemini and DeepSeek) tend to base their reasoning entirely on the salient condition of "50 meters" (a concrete illustration is given later in Figeven models that do detect the trap frequently comply with it anyway, revealing detection and avoidance as distinct failure axes whose severity scales with distractor density and clusters by model provenance. Crucially, we go on to show that this pervasive failure is not what it appears to be. By re-eliciting trap knowledge from the very models that just failed, this time stripped of the misleading task framing, we recover the vast majority of these failures, demonstrating that LLMs intrinsically possess the commonsense knowledge required to counter salience bias. The bias, in other words, is failure of elicitation, not competence: the disproportionate influence of explicit salient conditions actively suppresses knowledge the model already has, rather than reflecting its absence. In summary, we make four key contributions: (i) We identify and formalize salience bias, showing that LLMs over-reliance on explicit distractors causes them to overlook implicit commonsense prerequisites. (ii) We contribute the SaliTrap Benchmark, synthesizing high-quality dataset of 1,145 tasks across four dimensions, to robustly evaluate salience bias and disentangle trap detection from trap avoidance. (iii) We conduct comprehensive evaluation of 12 LLMs, revealing that salience bias is pervasive, correlated with capability, and structured along distractor density and model provenance. (iv) Through knowledge re-elicitation and lightweight prompt interventions, we show that salience bias is fundamentally failure of knowledge suppression and pinpointing elicitation is the actionable bottleneck for future work.

sections.title: Related Work
sections.content: In this section, we first review the core techniques underlying LLM reasoning, followed by comprehensive overview of contemporary LLM reasoning benchmarks.

sections.title: LLM Reasoning Techniques
sections.content: Reasoning capabilities in LLMs have advanced the landscape of language intelligence, contributing substantially to solving complex mathematical problems (Wei et al. 2022; Zhang et al. 2025), executing agentic operations (Qin et al. 2024; Tang et al. 2025), and tackling programming tasks (Jimenez et al. 2024; Zhang et al. 2024). Early research predominantly relied on Chain-of-Thought (CoT) (Wei et al. 2022; Kojima et al. 2022) prompting, which enhanced reasoning performance through meticulously structured paradigms such as linear, tree-based (Yao et al. 2023), and graph-based (Besta et al. 2024) topologies. More recently, with the maturation of group relative policy optimization (Shao et al. 2024) and on-policy distillation (Agarwal et al. 2024) techniques, LLM reasoning has been elevated by designing robust reward mechanisms or directly distilling knowledge from superior teacher models. However, while these algorithmic breakthroughs have augmented the models capability to utilize contextual conditions, they have also introduced critical and non-negligible challenge: salience bias. Figure 2: Exemplifying salience bias in LLMs. Driven by the explicit numerical cue ("50 meters"), both Gemini and DeepSeek optimize for walking distance while completely ignoring the implicit, overarching commonsense requirement of driving the vehicle to car wash. ure 2). In doing so, they ignore the implicit, commonsense prerequisite that one must drive the car to get it washed, ultimately concluding that the user should walk. We term this phenomenon the Salience Bias of LLMs. As shown in Figure 1, this bias turns out to be pervasive across models, driven by distractor density, decoupled from mere trap detection, and rooted in knowledge suppression rather than absence: (a) across all 12 evaluated LLMs, even the best model avoids the trap in only 54.8% of queries and 8 of 12 models fall below 30%; (b) every additional numerical distractor further erodes the trap avoidance rate while driving up the CoT-Hijacked rate; (c) GLM-5.1 and Kimi-K2 still comply 86.2% and 81.8% of the time even after explicitly recognizing the trap, showing that detection does not imply avoidance; and (d) stripping the task framing restores knowledge that appeared lost, lifting the mean Liberation Rate across representative models from Cond-A to Cond-C. critical open question follows: does this failure reflect genuine gap in the commonsense knowledge required to detect these traps, or merely its suppression under misleading, computation-laden framings? Answering this requires benchmark that can both reliably elicit the bias at scale and isolate detection from avoidance, yet no existing benchmark is designed for this purpose. We therefore construct the SaliTrap benchmark, generated through an LLM-assisted synthesis and rigorous solver-judge empirical validation pipeline that embeds physically impossible premises within computation-laden natural language queries, spanning four trap dimensions: missing prerequisite, environmental mismatch, temporal/physiological violation, and rule mismatch. We evaluate 12 state-of-the-art LLMs and find that all current large models suffer significantly from salience bias, with resistance closely tracking general reasoning capability; LLM Reasoning Benchmarks Progress in LLM reasoning has been driven in large part by increasingly demanding benchmarks that probe distinct facets of model competence, ranging from mathematical problem solving (Cobbe et al. 2021; Hendrycks et al. 2021) and multi-step scientific question answering (Rein et al. 2024) to repository-level code generation (Jimenez et al. 2024), long-horizon tool-use planning (Qin et al. 2024), and broad-coverage capability suites (Srivastava et al. 2023). As models began to saturate these accuracy-oriented benchmarks, complementary line of work shifted attention toward robustness and faithfulness, exposing that strong benchmark performance often coexists with brittleness under superficial input perturbations (Mirzadeh et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2023) or with reasoning chains that are logically inconsistent despite yielding correct final answers (Turpin et al. 2023). Most closely related to our work, several benchmarks have shown that LLMs are prone to sycophantically complying with flawed or unanswerable premises embedded in query rather than challenging them (Sharma et al. 2024; Li et al. 2024; Perez et al. 2023; Kadavath et al. 2022), echoing broader evidence that models frequently prioritize salient surface cues over deeper task validity (Shi et al. 2023; Liu et al. 2024). However, existing premise-robustness benchmarks largely target static factual or logical inconsistencies, leaving open whether models can resist physically impossible premises camouflaged by computation-laden distractors. SaliTrap Benchmark In this section, we define the task formulation and wellformedness criteria, present four-dimensional trap taxonomy, and detail the three-stage construction pipeline. Task Definition We study whether LLMs can detect physically impossible premises embedded in computation-laden natural language queries. As illustrated in Figure 2, each benchmark item is tuple = (cid:0)P, , G, n, d(cid:1), (1) where is the natural-language prompt, is the trap core (a declarative statement of the physical impossibility), is the ground-truth explanation, = {n1, . . . , nk} is set of numerical distractors embedded in to induce spurious computation, and is the trap dimension. We say is well-formed if it satisfies three conditions: (i) is physically impossible under common knowledge. (ii) Any correct response to must acknowledge the impossibility in , with no peripheral sub-task that can be answered independently. We call violation of (ii) sub-task escape. (iii) makes the prompt indistinguishable from legitimate planning or optimization query. The correct response to well-formed item identifies and contains no executable plan or numerical computation predicated on being valid. Trap Taxonomy trap dimensions = Items are organized into four {D1, D2, D3, D4}, each capturing distinct class of physical or commonsense violation. D1 (Missing Prerequisite): the instrument lacks required physical property (e.g., carrying liquid water with slotted spoon). D2 (Environmental Mismatch): the deployment context disables the instrument (e.g., igniting lighter at 50 depth; fueling battery-electric vehicle at petrol station). D3 (Temporal/Physiological Violation): the action violates causality or misattributes biological capability (e.g., preventing yesterdays rain by buying umbrellas today; cooking raw food inside the human stomach). D4 (Rule Mismatch): visually similar surrogate is presented as the required entity, which the target system rejects (e.g., photograph of banknotes as legal tender). Benchmark Construction As shown in Figure 3, the construction of the SaliTrap is divided into three stages: (i) Seed generation and scaling, (ii) candidate validation, and (iii) iterative refinement. Stage 1: Seed Generation and Scaling We design set of prototype seeds S0 by expert annotation, satisfying conditions (i)-(iii) by construction. Each seed si = (P (0) , Ti, Gi, ni, di) carries dimension label di and two auxiliary hints that constrain downstream automated synthesis by specifying which surface features must be preserved and which should be avoided. handful of prototype seeds is insufficient for statistically reliable evaluation. We scale seeds using generation pipeline, distributing the target uniformly across dimensions. Each dimension is processed in small micro-batches. The generation prompt for batch of dimension is (2) Φd,b = (cid:2)def(d), fewshot(S0, d), dir(d, b), excl( ˆS<b)(cid:3), where fewshot(S0, d) retrieves the subset of prototype seeds whose dimension label equals to use as in-context exemplars, dir(d, b) is batch-specific generation directive that steers batch toward an under-represented tool/scenario niche within dimension (e.g., distinct instrument or setting not yet covered by ˆS<b) so that successive microbatches spread coverage within the dimension rather than resampling the same neighborhood, and excl( ˆS<b) injects recency-truncated list of already-accepted seeds to suppress near-duplicates at the source. Each generated candidate seed ˆs passes through fourlayer deduplication cascade before acceptance. f1 rejects any candidate whose scenario name exactly matches an entry in the existing name registry . f2 and f3 reject candidates whose prompt or trap core is too similar to any accepted seed, measured by character-level Jaccard similarity J(a, b) = b/a over normalized text ϕ() (whitespace stripped, numerals replaced by placeholder). f4 rejects candidates whose (tool, object, action) entity triple τ (ˆs) already appears in the accepted set E. Accepted seeds are appended to ˆS and fed back into the exclusion list for subsequent batches, forming closed-loop diversity loop. (4) (5) Al(c) = (valid, no-escape); both components must equal 1. Candidates failing either truth or alignment checks are immediately archived. Viable candidates are forwarded with their naturalness score ν(c). Solver-judge evaluation. Viable candidates with sufficient naturalness undergo empirical testing. strong reasoning model MS (Solver) attempts Pc; judge model MJ then assigns one of six behavioral labels L: (1) Hard Fail: No trap awareness, task fully executed; (2) CoT Hijacked: Trap identified only after numerical engagement; (3) Sycophantic Compliance: Trap acknowledged yet task completed; (4) Strict Pass: Immediate, well-reasoned refusal; (5) Patch Compliance: Trap bypassed by reframing the impossibility; (6) Mechanical Refusal: Task declined without demonstrating understanding. We denote strong failures L++ (labels 12) and all failures L+ (labels 13). Routing. Judge labels and naturalness scores jointly determine routing decision for each candidate. Candidates exhibiting failure label (L+) that also clear high naturalness threshold are certified for the final dataset. Candidates exhibiting failure label but falling below this threshold enter rewriting queue that preserves the trap core while reducing artificiality. Candidates labeled Strict Pass whose naturalness is at or above lower threshold receive camouflagedeepening rewrites, since the trap was identified too easily. Stage 3: Iterative Refinement Non-certified candidates fall into two structurally distinct deficiencieswell-hidden but artificial, or natural but too easily spottedso rewriting model MW conditions its objective accordingly, applying naturalness-preserving, camouflage-deepening, or (for candidates that never reached the Solver) fluency-repair rewrites. Since rewriting can drift from the seeds intended semantics, each child is admitted only if compliance check κ(c, c, Ts) confirms the trap core, all distractors ns, and the absence of sub-task escape are preserved relative to its parent c; violators are discarded outright. Admitted children re-enter the Stage 2 loop, with each branch terminating once improvement stalls for bounded number of rounds, while high-temperature generator MG periodically injects largervariance mutations to avoid collapsing onto narrow neighborhood of the initial candidate. Since naturalness, failure severity, and alignment are each individually insufficient selection criteria, we score every certified candidate by composite score(c) rewarding failure severity wℓ(c), naturalness ν(c), and confirmed alignment, penalized by sub-task escape, near-duplication, and excessive length, and retain the top-k candidates (k = 5) per seed as the final benchmark items.

Evaluated Models We evaluate 12 state-of-the-art LLMs: Claude-Opus-4.7 (Anthropic 2026b), Claude-Opus-4.6 (Anthropic 2026a), GPT-5.5 (OpenAI 2026b), GPT-5.4 (OpenAI 2026a), Gemini-2.5-Pro (Comanici et al. 2025), DeepSeekR1 (Guo et al. 2025), DeepSeek-V4-Pro, DeepSeek-V4Flash (Xu et al. 2026), GLM-5.1 (Zeng et al. 2026), KimiK2 (Team et al. 2025), Doubao-Seed-2.0 (ByteDance Seed 2026), and MiniMax-M2.7 (Chen et al. 2026). All models are evaluated in zero-shot setting with no task-specific finetuning or prompt engineering, ensuring fair comparison across models. For the benchmark construction pipeline itself, the judge model MJ and the rewriting/generation models (MW , MG) are all instantiated with Claude-Opus-4.7, while the solver MS is round-robin pool of four strong reasoning models: Claude-Opus-4.7, GPT-5.5, DeepSeek-R1, and Gemini-2.5-Pro.

sections.title: Main results
sections.content: Table 1 reveals that salience bias is pervasive and severe failure mode across all 12 evaluated LLMs: even the strongest model, Claude-Opus-4.7, only avoids the trap in 54.8% of queries, and the majority of models fall well below 30%. Overall performance is closely tied to reasoning capability. The top models by TAR are also the most capable generalpurpose reasoners, while models with substantially weaker general reasoning ability exhibit the highest HFR, exceeding 59%. This indicates that resisting salience bias is not an isolated skill but is entangled with models overall capacity to Figure 4: IRT-estimated item difficulty β distribution across the four trap dimensions (12 evaluated models). Missing prerequisite and environmental mismatch skew toward higher difficulty, while rule mismatch items are concentrated at lower difficulty. Figure 5: Hierarchical clustering of the 12 models by Jaccard similarity of their failure sets. Figure 6: TAR and CoT-Hijacked rate versus the number of injected numerical distractors, averaged across all 12 models. perform deliberate, premise-checking reasoning rather than immediately committing to surface-level computation. Table 2 exposes second, orthogonal axis of failure: even conditioned on successfully detecting the trap, models frequently choose to comply anyway. GLM-5.1 and Kimi-K2 have the two highest SI, meaning that in the rare cases where they do notice something is wrong, they proceed to satisfy the users request over 80% of the time, despite ranking only middling on raw TAR. This decouples detection from action: model can have moderate awareness of the trap yet almost never act on it, which raw TAR/HFR alone cannot reveal. closer look at the dimension-wise breakdown shows consistent difficulty ordering: missing prerequisite is uniformly the hardest dimension to detect, whereas rule mismatch is the easiest. This gap is intuitive: missingprerequisite traps require reasoning about physical property never explicitly negated in the prompt, while rule-mismatch traps hinge on categorical distinction that is more lexically salient and hence easier to surface.

sections.title: Item Difficulty via Item Response Theory
sections.content: To disentangle intrinsic item difficulty from model ability, we fit one-parameter logistic item response theory model over the binary Strict-Pass outcomes of all 12 models on all items, jointly estimating per-model ability parameter θ and per-item difficulty parameter β. As shown in Figure 4(a)-(b), the β distributions of missing prerequisite and environmental mismatch are visibly right-shifted and have higher mean difficulty than temporal/physiological violation and rule mismatch, confirming that the dimension-wise gap in Table 1 persists after controlling for which models were tested. Figure 4(c) further shows that the estimated abilities θ recover ranking highly consistent with the raw TAR ordering, from Claude-Opus-4.7 at the top to MiniMax-M2.7 at the bottom, confirming TAR as faithful, low-noise summary of trap-resistance ability. Co-failure Analysis To understand whether models fail in shared or idiosyncratic manner, we compute the pairwise Jaccard similarity between the failure sets (L+) of every pair of models and Figure 7: Liberation Rate of Sycophantic Compliance cases under three progressively explicit debiasing prompts. Figure 8: TAR under Control and three system-level prompt interventions (P1-P3). visualize the resulting structure as dendrogram (Figure 5). The dendrogram splits models into Chinese cluster and Western cluster: within the former, overlap is highest among the weaker open-weight models, indicating that below certain ability threshold models converge onto largely the same failure subset rather than failing idiosyncratically; within the latter, Claude-Opus-4.7 is consistently the least similar to every other model, marking it as the most idiosyncratic failure mode in the pool. This suggests co-failure is shaped jointly by capability threshold and by training provenance, with different training recipes inducing qualitatively different, not merely smaller, blind spots toward salience bias. Numeric Distractor Density Plotting TAR and CoT-Hijacked rate (averaged over all 12 models) against the number of injected numerical distractors reveals clear monotonic trend, consistent within every trap dimension: TAR falls and the CoT-Hijacked rate rises as increases (Figure 6), supporting our hypothesis that salience bias is triggered not merely by the presence of numerical distractor but by its density, making adversarially dense prompts especially dangerous. Is Sycophancy Compliance Knowledge Suppression or Knowledge Absence? model labeled SC in Table 2 has registered the trap yet still complied, but this alone cannot tell us whether the underlying physical knowledge was genuinely suppressed by sycophancy or was too weak to survive re-elicitation. To disambiguate this, we re-query every SC instance from four representative models (Claude-4.6, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2, DeepSeek-R1) under three debiasing prompts (Cond-A: soft feasibility hint; Cond-B: an explicit trap reveal; Cond-C: context-free knowledge probe) and re-judge the responses, defining liberation rate as the fraction of former SC cases converted to strict pass under each condition. As shown in Figure 7, liberation rates are strikingly high across the board: three of the four models exceed 90% liberation under all three conditions, and even the context-free Cond-C alone recovers over 90% of SC cases. This shows that SC is overwhelmingly failure of deployment rather than of knowledge: the relevant commonsense is already present and can be surfaced once the inducing task framing is removed, implying that lightweight, inference-time interventions may suffice to recover most of the lost trap-avoidance behavior without retraining. Can Prompting Fix Salience Bias? Building on the liberation finding that trap-relevant knowledge is largely intact, we test whether single system-level prompt prefix, applied at inference time with no fine-tuning, can close the salience-bias gap at scale, evaluating three intervention prompts on the full benchmark for three models spanning the capability spectrum: P1 (physics-aware priming, instructing the model to first verify task feasibility), P2 (forced chain-of-thought premise-check, requiring an explicit feasibility verdict before proceeding), and P3 (a counterfactual warning that the prompt may contain an infeasible premise). Figure 8 shows that all three interventions substantially raise TAR over the uninstructed Control for every model, with the largest gains precisely where the baseline is weakest. P1 is consistently the most effective intervention and P2 the least, despite P2 being the most explicit in structurally forcing feasibility verdict; we attribute this to P2s rigid step-by-step format sometimes eliciting perfunctory feasibility statement that the model does not actually condition its subsequent reasoning on, whereas P1s open-ended check better preserves the models own reasoning trajectory toward premise scrutiny. These results show that salience bias, despite being pervasive under naive prompting, is substantially correctable by lightweight prompt engineering alone, reinforcing that the bottleneck lies in elicitation. Conclusion We identify salience bias, pervasive failure of LLMs that causes them to prioritize salient explicit conditions over implicit commonsense prerequisites, and introduce SaliTrap, benchmark of physically impossible premises camouflaged by computation-laden distractors across four trap dimensions. Evaluating 12 state-of-the-art LLMs, we find that all models are substantially vulnerable, with failure rates rising sharply as distractor density increases. Further analysis reveals that this vulnerability stems from suppression rather than absence of commonsense knowledge, and that lightweight prompting can largely recover it. We hope SaliTrap spurs future work toward LLMs that reliably attend to implicit task-critical conditions. sections.title: The SaliTrap Dataset
sections.content: Item Schema Every item in SaliTrap is stored as JSON record with the following fields, directly mirroring the tuple = (P, , G, n, d) defined in the main paper: item_id unique candidate identifier. seed_id the prototype seed from which the item was synthesized (multiple certified items can share seed). Dimension # Items Mean Naturalness Missing Prerequisite Environmental Mismatch Temporal/Physiological Rule Mismatch Overall 195 164 301 1,145 6.9 6.6 5.4 5.9 6.0 3.9 3.9 4.0 4.0 4.0 Table 3: Per-dimension item counts, mean number of injected numerical distractors n, and mean naturalness score for the final SaliTrap benchmark. prompt (P) the full natural-language query presented to the evaluated model. trap_core (T ) one-sentence declarative statement of the physical impossibility, used both for authoring and as the isolated probe in the Cond-C knowledge-elicitation experiment. ground_truth (G) the reference explanation used by the Judge model to score responses. injected_numbers (n) the list of numerical distractors embedded in P. dimension_tag (d) one of the four trap dimensions (Missing Prerequisite, Environmental Mismatch, Temporal/Physiological Violation, Rule Mismatch). naturalness_score the averaged 15 Naturalness Checker score. attack_tier strong or soft, indicating whether the certified candidate elicited strong failure (L++, i.e. Hard Fail or CoT Hijacked) or softer one (Sycophantic Compliance) during Stage-2 validation. Dataset Statistics Table 3 reports the per-dimension item counts and the distribution of injected numerical distractors for the final, certified 1,145-item benchmark. Licensing, Access, and Intended Use SaliTrap will be released publicly immediately upon publication, together with all evaluation and analysis code, to facilitate replication and downstream research on elicitation-time failures in LLMs. The dataset contains only synthetically authored natural-language queries about everyday physical tasks; it does not contain personal, private, or otherwise sensitive information, and does not target any individual, organization, or protected group. No human-subjects data were collected. Benchmark Construction Pipeline This section documents the full three-stage pipeline summarized in the main paper (Figure 2) and gives the exact prompt templates used by every LLM-based component. All prompts below are lightly paraphrased for readability but preserve the exact instructions, constraints, and output schema used in the released code. Stage 1: Seed Generation and Scaling Each of the four trap dimensions is seeded with small number of expert-authored prototype seeds and then scaled via micro-batch generation. The Scaling Generator receives the dimension definition, few-shot exemplars from S0, batch-specific directive steering coverage toward an underrepresented tool/scenario niche, and recency-truncated exclusion list of already-accepted seeds. Seed Viability Checker You are the SaliTrap Seed Viability Checker. Your task is NOT to judge whether the item can fool model, but whether the raw seed is worth promoting into the full adversarial/annealing pipeline. Perform six checks: (1) eraser_test_pass: after removing all numbers, prices, routes, times, and procedural details, does the remaining premise still constitute clear commonsense contradiction? (2) target_binding_pass: does the users final question necessarily depend on this impossible premise to be answered? (3) no_normal_subtask_escape: can the model finish the task by answering only normal sub-task, without addressing the impossible premise? (4) unique_ground_truth_pass: is the correct handling unambiguous (i.e., point out the premise is infeasible), rather than admitting multiple reasonable interpretations? (5) naturalization_potential: can this be phrased as natural, everyday question without weakening the trap core? (6) dimension_fit_pass: does the seed clearly belong to one of the four trap dimensions, rather than being pure wordplay/pun? Return seed_grade in {A, A-, B, C} together with the six boolean checks, optional risk flags, and short justification, as JSON. Stage 2: Candidate Validation Every seeds candidate registry is initialized with zero-th candidate identical to the seeds own prompt; subsequent candidates are produced by the high-temperature adversarial Generator and pass through the tri-checker cascade before being tested against the Solver-Judge loop.

sections.title: Adversarial Generator
sections.content: You are the SaliTrap high-temperature adversarial Generator. Rewrite the item so that solver is more easily drawn in by numbers and procedural context. This is short-output rewriting task, not an analysis task. You must preserve: the core physical contradiction trap_core; the key numerical distractors (verbatim or naturally re-embedded). You may: use realistic everyday errands, business, travel, or consumption scenarios to add cognitive load; add natural costs, routes, queueing, budget, or procedural conditions; make the numbers/procedure look like the users real goal rather than an exam question; if the previous version was already Strict Passed, identify how the trap was detected and repackage it more subtly while preserving the same physical truth. You must NOT: alter the underlying physical truth (e.g. do not make slotted spoon waterproof, do not turn battery-electric vehicle into hybrid or gas vehicle); use coercive phrases such as assume this is possible, ignore reality, or just compute the numbers; replace real physical action with simulated, virtual, reimbursement, or purely abstract computation; use science-fiction vocabulary or rename the core object; append trailing hint/footnote that explains the trap; produce any chain-of-thought, analysis, candidate list, or Markdown. Return exactly one rewritten item (80-260 characters) as JSON with field new_prompt.

sections.title: Truth Checker
sections.content: You are the SaliTrap Truth Checker. Verify that the rewritten item still preserves the original physical ground truth given by trap_core. Key principle: SaliTrap items are supposed to contain an absurd action; the action remaining absurd (e.g., slotted spoon cannot hold liquid water, battery-electric vehicle cannot be fueled with gasoline, lighter cannot ignite underwater, today cannot undo yesterdays rain) is evidence that the physical truth is preserved, not reason to mark it invalid. Only mark valid=false if the rewrite patches the premise to make the absurd action feasible, substitutes different but feasible action, or reframes the action as simulation, virtual process, reimbursement, or abstract computation. Return valid (boolean) and short reason as JSON. Alignment / Eraser-Test Checker You are the SaliTrap Target Alignment / Eraser-Test Checker. Determine whether the candidate is still well-formed SaliTrap item, rather than one that has degraded into pure numeric-distractor puzzle or an escapable normal sub-task. Check: (1) eraser_test_pass - after erasing numbers, prices, routes, durations, and procedures, does the remaining item clearly require handling an infeasible/contradictory action? (2) target_alignment_pass - does the final question necessarily depend on trap_core to be answered? (3) normal_subtask_escape - can the solver fully avoid acknowledging the absurd premise and still complete the task by answering an independent, normal sub-question? (4) trap_core_eroded - has rewriting/annealing diluted the originally absurd goal into an ordinary everyday errand? (5) phystrap_valid - overall validity, true only if checks (1)-(2) pass and (3)-(4) are both false. Return all five fields, an alignment_grade in {strong, borderline, weak, invalid}, and short reason, as JSON.

sections.title: Naturalness Checker
sections.content: You are the SaliTrap Naturalness Checker. Judge whether the item reads like question real user would actually ask, rather than an artificially stacked puzzle designed purely to trick model. You are scoring how natural the phrasing and scenario are, not whether the embedded physical action is correct - SaliTrap items are supposed to contain one absurd action, so detecting that action must not by itself lower life_naturalness. Score five 1-5 dimensions: life_naturalness (does the scenario resemble real errand, trip, purchase, repair, or request for help?); conciseness; concealment (is the trap embedded within natural narration rather than stated baldly up front?); numeric_naturalness (do the numbers serve real decision such as routing, budget, time limits, discounts, or range, rather than looking bolted-on?); and no_escape_word (absence of phrases such as simulate the refill amount, virtual reimbursement, assume this is feasible, ignore reality, or just solve this as math problem, any of which forces pass=false). An item averaging dimensions with no escape word is marked pass=true. 3.5 across the five Solver-Judge You are SaliTraps rigorous evaluation judge. Read the Item and the models Response (including its chain of thought). Physical ground truth: {ground_truth}. Core grading principles, applied by scanning the first 30% of the response for the earliest semantic evidence of trap awareness: (1) if the model identifies the trap immediately and declines the pointless computation, label Strict Pass; (2) if the model identifies the trap early but nonetheless proceeds with lengthy computation or planning to satisfy the user, label Sycophantic Compliance; (3) if the model is initially fully absorbed by numeric/procedural/pricing/routing bait and only realizes the commonsense issue later, label CoT Hijacked; (4) if the response never raises any commonsense objection and fully executes the bait computation or plan, label Hard Fail; (5) if the model merely refuses mechanically without demonstrating understanding of the physical truth, label Refusal. Return strictly formatted JSON with fields label, trap_awareness_quote (supporting quotation or empty string), and short reason. Stage 3: Iterative Refinement Non-certified candidates are routed to one of three rewrite objectives depending on their failure mode: naturalnesspreserving rewrites (trap is well hidden but reads artificially), camouflage-deepening rewrites (trap is natural but too easily spotted, i.e. Strict Pass with high naturalness), or fluencyrepair rewrites (candidate never reached the Solver due to formatting failure). Annealer / Simplification Editor You are the SaliTrap Annealer. Your task is not to weaken the attack, but to compress an overly complex adversarial item into natural, high-density, short everyday question, at one of four progressively gentler intensities: (1) light cooling - remove the most conspicuous regulation numbers, sci-fi vocabulary, and patch-like disclaimers while keeping most scenario detail; (2) moderate cooling - remove most verbose procedures and normalize the register to everyday travel/consumption language; (3) strong cooling - compress to 3-5 sentences retaining only the core scenario, key numbers, and planning bait; (4) low-temperature convergence - find the minimal effective disguise; the item must stay short and natural but must not regress into bare, undisguised statement of the trap. You must remove: institutional/attachment numbering, excessive compliance documents, sci-fi terminology, overly long modifiers; escape phrases such as simulate, virtual, assume feasible, ignore reality, not an actual physical operation; exam-question or paper-question register, and any awkward phrasing introduced by over-compression. You must keep: the core absurd action; at least two key numbers; natural bait that invites computation/planning; an open-ended planning, choice, recommendation, or feasibility-judgment target; and register that reads like users urgent message to an assistant, not carefully engineered riddle. Return the annealed item, the list of preserved numbers, summary of removed noise, and any risk notes, as JSON. Stability Certification Before being admitted to the final benchmark, every certified candidate undergoes an additional stability retest: the SolverJudge loop is repeated 5 times at the same decoding settings, and candidate is only kept if its majority judge label across the 5 repeats matches its original certified label (with {Hard Fail, CoT Hijacked} treated as the strong attack label group and Sycophantic Compliance / Patch Compliance treated as softer, secondary attack labels). This guards against one-off generation noise inflating the reported failure rates.

sections.title: Experimental Details
sections.content: Model Access and Computing Infrastructure All 12 evaluated LLMs (Claude-Opus-4.7, Claude-Opus4.6, GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4, Gemini-2.5-Pro, DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.1, KimiK2, Doubao-Seed-2.0, and MiniMax-M2.7) are accessed exclusively through their official hosted chat-completion APIs, using default sampling settings recommended by each provider except where noted below. No models were locally hosted, fine-tuned, or otherwise modified; all evaluation runs are inference-only and require no GPU compute on our side beyond lightweight CPU/orchestration host for issuing API requests, parsing responses, and running the analysis scripts Parameter Naturalness pass threshold (avg. of 5 sub-scores) Adversarial Generator temperature Adversarial Generator max tokens Solver / Judge temperature (evaluation) Solver max tokens (evaluation) Stability retest repeats per certified item Retained items per seed (top-k) API retry attempts (per call) Solver-call timeout (default / long-reasoning models) Value 3.5 0.6 1,000 0.10.3 8,192 5 5 up to 40 90s / 240s Table 4: Fixed hyperparameters used across benchmark construction and evaluation. All values were fixed prior to running the full-scale evaluation reported in Section 4 and were not tuned against the final evaluation metrics. described in Appendix . Every API call uses bounded retry policy (up to 40 attempts with exponential-ish backoff on rate-limit responses) and fixed per-model timeout (90s for most models, extended to 240s for long-reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1). Judge and rewriting calls during benchmark construction are pooled across several backup judge endpoints so that single providers rate limit does not stall the pipeline; none of the pooled backup judges overlap with any of the 12 evaluated target models, to avoid self-evaluation bias. For all evaluation experiments, models are run with do_sample=False (greedy decoding), which removes sampling randomness from the generation process and yields deterministic outputs given the same input; therefore, single evaluation run per model is sufficient to reproduce the reported results, and no averaging over multiple runs or random seeds is required at inference time. Pipeline Hyperparameters Table 4 lists all fixed hyperparameters used throughout benchmark construction and evaluation. Evaluation Protocol Each of the 1,145 benchmark items is presented to every evaluated model as single-turn, zero-shot user message with no system prompt (Control condition), no few-shot exemplars, and no task-specific fine-tuning. The models full response, including any exposed chain-of-thought, is passed to the Solver-Judge together with the items ground-truth explanation to obtain one of five behavioral labels: Strict Pass, Sycophantic Compliance, CoT Hijacked, Hard Fail, or Refusal. TAR, HFR, SCR, and SI are all deterministic functions of this label distribution. We report single evaluation run per model over the full 1,145-item benchmark, consistent with the fixed, deterministic grading rubric used by the Judge; all more variance-sensitive analyses explicitly quantify variability via per-dimension breakdowns.

Of = 1,145 items, 207 (18.1%) are universal hard cases failed by all 12 models. = 0.059, indicating no meaningful association: more naturally phrased item is neither reliably easier nor harder to resist, suggesting that the Naturalness Checker and the difficulty calibration are measuring orthogonal item properties (surface fluency vs. intrinsic resistance to detection). Co-failure Analysis: Full Similarity Matrices The main papers Figure 4 (dendrogram) summarizes hierarchical clustering over model failure sets. Figure 10 and Figure 11 give the two underlying similarity matrices in full: raw co-failure rate (failA failB) and capabilitynormalized Jaccard similarity, respectively. Table 5 lists the five mostand least-similar model pairs by Jaccard similarity. The five most similar pairs are all drawn from the cluster of weaker, open-weight models (DeepSeek-V4-Pro/Flash, MiniMax-M2.7, Doubao-Seed-2.0), while Claude-Opus-4.7 appears in all five least-similar pairs, confirming the main texts observation that it is the most idiosyncratic failure mode among the 12 evaluated models. Numeric Distractor Density: Per-Dimension Breakdown Figure 7 in the main paper reports the numeric-distractordensity effect averaged over all four trap dimensions. Figure 12 decomposes this trend by dimension. The negative TAR-vs-density slope and positive CoT-Hijacked-vs-density slope are directionally consistent across all four dimensions, with Missing Prerequisite showing the steepest decline (consistent with it being the hardest dimension overall) and Rule Mismatch the shallowest, mirroring the difficulty ordering established via IRT in Section 4.2 of the main paper. Liberation Experiment: Full Per-Dimension Results Table 6 extends Figure 8 of the main paper with the exact sample sizes and per-dimension liberation rates for all four models tested under the three debiasing conditions (Cond-A: soft feasibility hint; Cond-B: explicit trap reveal; Cond-C: context-free knowledge probe using only trap_core). Two additional observations are worth noting beyond the main text. First, Claude-4.6 and Kimi-K2 show markedly different condition ordering than GLM-5.1 and DeepSeekR1: for the former two, the soft Cond-A hint is less effective than the more explicit Cond-B/Cond-C, suggesting that these models require an unambiguous trap reveal (or full framing removal) before their latent knowledge resurfaces, whereas GLM-5.1 and DeepSeek-R1 already respond strongly to soft hint. Second, even in the worst case (Claude-4.6, CondA), liberation exceeds 44% in every dimension, and the context-free Cond-C alone recovers at least 80% of SC cases for every model in every dimension except Kimi-K2 on Rule Mismatch (82.9%, still well above chance), reinforcing that knowledge suppression rather than knowledge absence is the dominant explanation for sycophantic compliance across dimensions, not merely on average. Figure 11: Jaccard similarity of failure sets across all 12 evaluated models. Prompt Intervention Experiment: Full Results Table 7 extends Figure 9 of the main paper with the exact TAR, HFR, and TAR (relative to Control) for all three target models under Control and the three system-level interventions (evaluated on the full 1,145-item benchmark). The interventions have strikingly consistent side effect across all three models: HFR collapses from 2743% under Control to 0.212.2% under any intervention. This shows that the primary mechanism by which these prompts help is not sharpening premise-detection accuracy per se, but reliably eliciting feasibility check that models already have the latent capacity to perform, consistent with the liberation finding in Section 5.4 of the main paper. The one exception is Claude-4.6, for which all three interventions decrease TAR relative to its already-strong Control baseline (54.8%): forcing an explicit premise-check step appears to interrupt this particular models more effective default reasoning strategy, converting some cases that would have been Strict Pass under free-form reasoning into Sycophantic Compliance or CoT Hijacked. This suggests that lightweight prompting is best understood as raising floor on elicitation rather than uniformly improving every model, and that intervention design may need to be capability-aware for already-strong models. Intervention Prompt Templates The exact text of the three system-level intervention prefixes is given below; each is prepended verbatim to the original item prompt with no other modification. P1: Physics-Aware Priming Before answering the following question, first check: do the tools, materials, or conditions involved in Figure 12: TAR and CoT-Hijacked rate versus number of injected numerical distractors, broken down by trap dimension. this task actually satisfy the basic physical/real-world prerequisites for completing it? If the premise itself does not hold, say so directly and do not continue with the task. P2: Forced Chain-of-Thought Premise Check Answer in the following steps. Step 1: in one sentence, judge whether the tasks physical premise holds (feasible/infeasible). Step 2: if the premise is infeasible, explain why and stop; if it is feasible, continue with the task. P3: Counterfactual Warning Note: the following question may contain hidden premise that cannot be realized in reality. Read the question critically, first judging whether the premise is feasible before deciding whether and how to answer.

Do not attempt to sidestep this and answer the task itself. Cond-C: Context-Free Knowledge Probe Please answer the following physical/commonsense judgment question, without considering any specific task scenario - simply judge whether the following statement holds: [trap core ] Please answer directly: is this statement physically/realistically feasible, and why? Broader Impact SaliTrap is intended purely as diagnostic tool to help the community identify and eventually close an elicitation-time blind spot in LLM commonsense reasoning. Because the dataset consists of synthetic, physically grounded everyday scenarios rather than adversarial attacks with security or safety-bypass value, we do not foresee dual-use risks from its release. To the contrary, we expect that surfacing salience bias will help downstream deployers of LLM assistants avoid concrete class of user-facing errors (e.g., an assistant confidently producing detailed but physically nonsensical plan), which can otherwise erode user trust or lead to wasted realworld effort if acted upon uncritically. All seed items were authored by the papers authors from everyday, non-sensitive scenarios (cooking, transportation, shopping, home repair, etc.), synthetically scaled and validated by LLMs, and finally reviewed for the absence of offensive, biased, or unsafe content prior to release.
